newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh forest threatened by blazing gas well.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh forest threatened by blazing gas well.

text.p: Workers struggled on Thursday to keep a raging gas well fire from reaching a rich timber forest in northeast Bangladesh.

Men worked feverishly chopping down trees around the burning well to create a firebreak to stop the fire from spreading, but local officials warned they did not have the resources to battle a major forest fire.
"The large, thick forest surrounding the fire site is under serious threat," Badrul Anam, Assistant Conservationist from the Sylhet Forest, told Reuters.
"We are worried what would happen in the scorching summer heat if a big wind comes up -- the flames are drying leaves and branches and can spark fire any time. It will be a disaster then," he said.
The 10,000-acre reserve forest surrounding the field is rich with timber planted since the early 1920s.
Mohammad Atiqul Azam, a divisional forest officer in Sylhet, said a preliminary damage assessment would be ready in two days.

"We don't know what the (biological) impact will be as it depends how long the fire will rage. But as of now we are fearing major damage... I am afraid it may take many years for the area to recover."

Fire-fighting experts arrived at the gas field from Singapore on Tuesday and another team from the U.S. headquarters of Occidental Petroleum Corporation was expected to join them later in the day, energy ministry officials said.

Earlier, an Occidental official said it could take weeks to put the fire out. It has already destroyed parts of two nearby tea gardsens and plantations. "They (the fire-fighting experts) are here but it remains to be seen how much they can help," said an official in Moulvi Bazar, a tea-growing district where the field is located.
An explosion triggered the blaze on Sunday. Occidental Petroleum Corporation began drilling the well earlier this month.

Forestry workers were unable to approach the fire because of flames leaping 300 to 500 feet (100 to 150 metres) in the air. Four Bangladeshis were hurt in the first days of the blaze and nearby railway tracks also caught fire.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina visited the area on Tuesday and urged residents to stay calm.
"It's major accident, but such accidents occurs in other countries too," the prime minister told residents in Mugrachhara.

"Face the situation with courage and patience. Don't panic. Everything possible is being done to cope with the situation," Hasina said. Occidental had already invested $10 million in the exploration and planned to spend up to $100 million to explore three of 23 blocks that Bangladesh had earmarked for foreign firms.
